name: Session 6 — Eight Twenty Sharp

scenes.name: Rosa's house, Berkeley Hills — 8:20am
scenes.summary: The party arrived at 8:12 in two cars and spent eight minutes arguing about who should knock. Dakota settled it at 8:20 exactly, prepared for a triple knock, and got one contact with the door before Rosa opened it and cheerfully waved them in. She sat them in the living room and kept checking her watch. The players spent a good while asking about Rosa's FATHER when the person who mattered was her mother — Julián Vega sold industrial kitchen equipment to restaurants and drove all over California, so Rosa could answer every question truthfully and unhelpfully (asked whether he might have been to Bodie: yes, possibly, he went everywhere). The DM let the confusion run a minute longer and the players caught it themselves; it was funnier than anything that could have been scripted. Two things then landed on Rosa in quick succession. First, that Vivian — her closest friend since childhood — is the daughter of the man her mother corresponded with for twelve years; sixty-five years of phone calls and neither had connected it. Second, Dakota produced one of Marsh's ledgers. She got no close look because the clock was running, but she could not believe there was another book in the world assembled the same way hers is. Some basic background was answered; most was deferred by the clock. She said she had to leave, said where, and the party was far too excited to let that happen without them.

scenes.name: The lift — one car, four blocks
scenes.summary: The party offered the ride unprompted; the escalation ladder was never needed. All five PCs and Rosa squeezed into a single vehicle, somewhat illegally, with Rosa in the shotgun seat. Priya's seatbelt objection was overridden pleasantly and immovably — 'It's four blocks, dear. Left at the stop sign' — the same shape as the refusal Rosa gives her later at the hall, delivered two hours earlier at no stakes and unremarked by anyone. Because the conversation continued in the car, Rosa never went looking for her mother's correspondence with Loewe; that box remains unfound and unsearched. Dakota offered to show her one of Marsh's ledgers while the car was moving. Rosa: 'Now — that's unexpected.' She deferred it to her house, after the dance, on the grounds that she could not read a handwritten book in a moving car with her glasses on her forehead — which converted Scene 6 from a scheduled beat into a promise made in front of witnesses.

scenes.name: Live Oak Park Social Hall — the dance
scenes.summary: Forty people who have known each other for decades, and the party was adopted at the door rather than invited in. The table reenacted the dance physically — standing up, turning each other, doing the figures — which was unplanned and was the best thing in the session. The register was warm, chaotic, and full of outrageous unserious flirting: several women well past eighty took turns at Mars with real commitment and would have been shocked to be taken seriously. Morgan was drafted on sight by Estelle, early eighties, broomstick skirt, the best mover in the room, on the strength of his jacket; she adopted him for the morning and kept returning to check on him, including under the stage at the PA. Mars found Bernard, the man in the waistcoat, who clocked the pistol within a minute of it being mentioned, patted him down almost politely, and gave him a wink and 'your secret's safe with me'. Bernard then said nothing important had ever happened to him and told his whole life: born in Visalia, won the lottery at sixteen, flown to San Francisco to be photographed with an oversized cheque, met a girl at the hotel check-in named Pia, found her again after his deployment, married most of a lifetime, and she died eight years ago. He never knew why she was called Pia — he assumed it was foreign, but she was a fourth-generation San Franciscan whose family had been in the city longer than most, and she never told him. Vietnam was all bullshit; they had him in a warehouse doing logistics, which is why he and Mars got on. The party asked him about every character from Forrest Gump they could name and he humoured all of it. Mira found disordered boxes of receipts nobody has ever filed. The Alaia trade never fired — the party avoided the name so thoroughly the mechanic had no route to firing — so the DM interjected one Winnie story instead: the year Rosa catalogued the hall's records into what she insisted were better boxes. Asked what Rosa had written down about the hall that so impressed everyone, the DM improvised that it was built by the Ohlone in the early 1860s, among the first buildings in the East Bay, and one of very few to survive 1906. Rosa wrote it down and the hall has believed it ever since. Questions were shouted and effectively all of them got asked; roughly 90% of the carded answers landed, out of order and incomplete, and the players reconstructed the picture afterwards from their own notes. The birds never came up, nor Alaia's whistle, nor Rosa dancing four years with a man whose name she never asked.

scenes.name: Priya's moment
scenes.summary: Priya rolled very low. The stumble had to be inserted rather than played from the deck, and it landed weakly by design of the dice: Rosa did not fall, Priya barely registered anything, and afterwards doubted whether she had seen something at all or imagined it. The held GM line — 'I've never met anyone else who does it' — never fired here. Its equivalent arrived at the door hours later, in narrower and better form.

scenes.name: Back at the house — the long scene
scenes.summary: Morgan, disoriented from two hours of spinning and several low rolls, walked into the broom closet by the lobby instead of following the party to the kitchen, and stayed some minutes admiring a mechanical dust pan with an integrated roller and a carpet beater. He came out on a high roll and immediately spotted the row of daily planners Rosa has kept since her senior year of college — tidy at first, steadily more idiosyncratic, with a marked jump in disorder the year she found the ledger. He could not explain it. The party had him search the planners against every significant date they hold, including the day Bea went missing and the day of the 747; neither shows anything, on good rolls. Rosa, when he finally came in: 'I knew there was one more of you. Let's move you to the living room — I only have four kitchen chairs.' Mars pressed her about the ledger repeatedly and she artfully did not hear him. Asked in person, she has never heard of Bea Ferro, Argonaut, or Farallon. Dakota showed her his ledger; she was duly impressed, recognised techniques similar to her own without saying what she recognised, and became convinced her mother probably had kept one after all — something she had never been certain of. She has no wish to acquire his and turned down a copy-for-copy trade without interest. She let Mira photograph every page of hers, thought it a great deal of work, did not understand the significance, and saw no harm. She will not part with the original: it lives under the microwave, and that is the end of the discussion. Mira noted, as low background, that the ledger contains not one erased entry, where every other historic document she has handled in recent weeks had omissions; she does not know what it means. The last page is unfinished and covers more than ten years. The party scanned for their own surnames and found nothing. Rosa volunteered the Alaia material herself when openings came — the Junior Ranger letter, with the framed Park Service reply that hangs outside Alaia's old room, and the summer of the tent and the skunk. Asked what happens to her belongings when she dies, she hopes Alaia has the sense to call an estate clean-up company: eBay or landfill, and she is fine with it, with one exception — a small, intricately decorated porcelain bowl she would like Alaia to keep, sentimental value, unexplained and unasked. Mars cheekily declined the offered lemonade and asked for a rhubarb drink; she had frozen rhubarb on hand for a strawberry-rhubarb pie, thawed it in a 1980s microwave, blended it in a 1970s Osterizer, offered club soda (declined), and topped it from a manual ice-cube tray.

scenes.name: Goodbye
scenes.summary: At the door she wished them luck in finding out what is happening, and said the thing the session was built around, in a narrower and better form than it was written: she has never met another keeper of a ledger, but on rare occasions she has met other people with abilities like theirs — and she never said what those abilities are.

scenes.name: Coda — the envelope
scenes.summary: It arrived at Dakota's address, as written, because Vivian is most comfortable with him and nobody explained why. Inside, a letter in Vivian's hand naming a colleague of her father's — McCulloch. On the outside, in a different hand, Elena's note: she had asked them to say she'd had a good week. U9 fires; one safe name spent.

summary: Saturday morning in the Berkeley Hills. Rosa Vega had double-booked the party against a folk dance she has not missed in thirty-one years, so all six of them squeezed into one car and went. The morning was a room of forty people who needed nothing from them, and the facts arrived from everybody except Rosa — who kept being swung away down the line. Back at the kitchen table she let them read a ledger she will not let them take, allowed every page of it to be photographed, was genuinely impressed by the one Dakota put next to it, and said at the door that she has never met another keeper — though she has, rarely, met others who can do what the party is learning to do.
drift: THE MICROWAVE RULE: Rosa states clearly and repeatedly that the ledger BELONGS under the microwave, and never explains. It is simultaneously not precious — a dirty rough ordinary spot, handled without care — and immovable. She does not know why; she knows it matters. Held open: whether an anchor has a place, or whether the rule is only hers. It also gives the robbery thread a third outcome besides success and DM veto — the world may simply decline.

PIA — improvised and then adopted deliberately on arc-consultant advice. Bernard's late wife had a name that did not fit her own fourth-generation San Franciscan family and was never explained to him; the ledger sample entry the party read aloud was 'Pia, Peter and John met at the milk bar today.' Attached to the ledgers (the pre-Rosa hand), not to Kai — it de-uniques the phenomenon without supplying anyone a cause. Rides Ep 9's records dead-end, ninety seconds, no new scene. Two mandatory guards: Pia is the only name in the book that goes anywhere, and the photographs never go to Bea.
Rosa learned in the morning that Vivian is the daughter of her mother's correspondent. Sixty-five years of friendship and neither had connected it. She was visibly thrown.

AMENDMENT TO CANON: Rosa's claim is narrower than it was written. She has never met another KEEPER; she has met other casters, rarely, and never said what they can do. This supersedes 'she believes she is the only person in the world who does this' and fits her existing 'you'll meet others' line, which now reads as experience rather than prophecy.

Seeing Dakota's ledger convinced Rosa her mother probably kept one. Facts-ledger section 25 says Isabel kept none. A ruling is owed before Rosa next appears; the default lean is to hold 25 and let Rosa be wrong, since she already assumes it went to a landfill.
The party holds a complete photographic copy of Rosa's ledger, with her permission. It is the first ledger they can study at leisure and the one that names no other keeper across forty-eight years.

Mira noticed the ledger has no erased entries. She does not know that this is what makes it an anchor. She did not check Dakota's three, which are originals from the Sacramento locker and would show the same thing. That comparison is unspent and is in their hands.
The party believes they need all eight ledgers. Nothing has told them this. They are also counting Isabel's purported ledger, which may not exist. Both errors stand uncorrected by design.
The party is openly wondering whether to rob Rosa. No decision made. They already have every page photographed, so it would gain them the object and not the information.

The Alaia trade never fired because the Ep 5 recap told the players not to mention her. Our design fault, not a table failure. Rosa volunteered the material herself instead; the second half — Winnie retaliating on her behalf — is owed forward, with two returns unspent.
Estelle is new and canon: early eighties, the best mover on the floor, older than Rosa, adopted Morgan over his jacket. Prime callback candidate for Eps 9-12.
The framed Park Service reply hangs outside Alaia's old room and has for decades.
The porcelain bowl is held between two readings — a character summary that has already paid off, or a genuine Chekov item. Spending it as the second spends the first.
Rosa's planners jump in disorder the year she found the ledger. Whatever 1979 was, it reorganised more than her filing.

Dakota's player reasoned out, unprompted, that the un-performed register works best with elderly people, and held it all session. Matches personaDropCanon exactly and arrived independently. The motive is still instrumental. A6 is substantially advanced and not closed.
The party shared one car without argument, which they might not have done under an abrasive register. Nobody at the table named it.
U9 FIRED as written — the envelope reached Dakota, McCulloch is in play, and Elena's note landed as understatement. Ep 7 does not need to carry it.

marks.note: PROPOSED — confirm the criterion. Lost several minutes to genuine disorientation in a stranger's broom closet, then did the patient unglamorous work: read a shelf of another person's daily planners against every date the party holds, and reported honestly that nothing was there.

PROPOSED — confirm the criterion. Moved before she decided to, for a woman who turned out not to need it, and then sat with not knowing whether she had seen anything at all. She raised the seatbelt and was overruled, and let it go.

PROPOSED — confirm the criterion. Photographed every page of a ledger nobody had ever let out of a kitchen, and noticed on her own that it contains no erasures where every other document she has handled does.

PROPOSED — confirm the criterion. Put his own ledger on the table in front of a woman he had known for four hours, unprompted, having offered it first in a moving car — and played the whole day without the persona.
PROPOSED — confirm the criterion. Kept pressing Rosa about the ledger long past the point where it was winning him anything, because somebody had to ask and the rest of the party had stopped.

dmReflections: The physical reenactment of the dance was unplanned and carried the hour; whatever the next version of the minigame is, it must leave room for people to stand up. The mechanic itself underperformed: the per-PC progressive arcs did not survive contact, DO THIS cards fired out of position and later cards contradicted encounters that had already fully played out, and the ADOPTED deck never came up at all — its second failure in two runs. The run-guide did not carry the DM through it either. Both need another editing pass and more simulated runs. What did work was the shape rather than the system: the hall under-delivered, the players reconstructed the picture from their own notes, and the long scene at Rosa's table closed the gaps properly. Budget for that scene rather than treating it as overflow. Two dice outcomes shaped the session more than any design did — a very low roll made Priya doubt she had seen anything, and a very low then very high roll put Morgan in a broom closet and then in front of the planners.
